passages.title: Email Correspondence: An Allotment Cultivation Notice

emails.subject: Plot 43B, Thornley Lane — cultivation notice dated 2 August
emails.body:
Dear Allotments Office,

I have received a cultivation notice for plot 43B stating that less than 50 per cent of the plot is under cultivation and that the tenancy will be terminated in 28 days unless this is remedied.

I am not disputing the measurement. Roughly a third of my plot is currently uncultivated, and I want to explain what is on it, because I think the assessment and the rule may be measuring different things.

That third is a wildflower and log-pile area I established two years ago, on the written advice of your own biodiversity officer, who visited the site in April and described it in her report as "exemplary". I have her email. It is not neglect and it is not couch grass; it is a deliberate habitat and it is the reason there are bees on the plots either side of mine.

My question is whether "cultivation" in the tenancy agreement means "planted with crops" or "actively managed". If it is the first, then the biodiversity officer's advice and the allotments rules contradict each other, and I would like that resolved rather than resolved against me in 28 days. If it is the second, then the notice was issued on a visual assessment that did not distinguish habitat from neglect, which is understandable and correctable.

I would rather have the definition than the plot, if it comes to it.

Sincerely,
Emiliano Vasquez-Ruiz

emails.subject: RE: Plot 43B, Thornley Lane — cultivation notice dated 2 August
emails.body:
Dear Mr Vasquez-Ruiz,

The notice is withdrawn, and the answer to your question is that we do not have one. That is the honest position and it is worse than either of your two options.

The tenancy agreement says "cultivated" and does not define it. The inspection sheet our officers carry says "planted or prepared for planting", which is narrower and was written by someone in 2011 who was not asked to write policy. So the rule that governs your tenancy and the rule your inspector applies are not the same rule, and neither is the rule our biodiversity officer works to. Three documents, one site, no agreement.

I have raised it for the tenancy review in October. I cannot promise the outcome — it will be decided by a committee I do not sit on, and I would rather tell you that than imply I can deliver a definition.

What I can do now: your plot is marked as inspected and compliant for this season, and the note on your file records the biodiversity officer's report so the next inspector sees it before the plot rather than after the notice.

One correction to something you may reasonably assume. Two other tenants received the same notice on 2 August for what looks like the same reason. I have not withdrawn theirs, because I do not know whether their uncultivated areas are habitat or neglect, and I am not going to assume either way. I am visiting both this week with the biodiversity officer.

Regards,
Margit Halvorsen
Allotments Officer

passages.title: Who Actually Has Access to Green Space
passages.content:
Cities report green space as a proportion of land area, and by that measure most perform reasonably. The measure conceals almost everything that determines whether a resident benefits from it, and the gap between the statistic and the experience is where most of the interesting findings sit.

Distance is the first distortion. Benefits associated with green space — physical activity, lower reported stress, cooler temperatures during heatwaves — depend on frequent use, and frequency falls sharply with distance. A large park two kilometres away and a small one five minutes' walk away are not equivalent inputs, and the second produces more measurable benefit despite contributing less to the headline figure. Cities can raise their green-space percentage by acquiring peripheral land while access for most residents is unchanged.

Distribution is uneven in a consistent direction. Neighbourhoods with lower incomes and higher housing density typically have less accessible green space per resident, which is the same population least likely to have a private garden and most exposed to summer heat. The disparity is well documented and it compounds: the same areas are hotter, and the cooling effect of tree canopy is one of the more reliable interventions available.

Perceived safety functions as a filter that the acreage figure cannot see. A park that women, older residents or parents with young children avoid after four o'clock in winter is available for a fraction of the hours it is open. Lighting, sightlines and the presence of other people determine effective access more than the boundary on a map, and improving them is often cheaper than acquiring land.

Quality and maintenance separate spaces that look identical in a survey. A field with no seating, no shade, no toilet and no water fountain is used differently from one with all four, particularly by older people and anyone with a health condition. These features rarely appear in green-space metrics and reliably appear in what users say determines whether they stay.

The conclusion the evidence supports is that the useful question is not how much green space a city has but how many residents can reach a usable, safe, maintained space within a short walk — a figure most cities do not publish and some do not calculate.

passages.title: Should Allotment Waiting Lists Be Managed by Splitting Plots?

viewpoints.name: Councillor Delphine Aubert
viewpoints.text: We halved plots on two sites to cut a nine-year waiting list and it worked on the metric we chose, which is the caveat I would attach to it. Twice as many households now hold a plot. What I did not anticipate is that a half plot cannot produce the volume that made the old plots worth the labour for some tenants, and we lost a number of long-standing growers who did not want a smaller one. The waiting list is shorter and the site is different. I would still do it, and I would say both halves of that out loud.

viewpoints.name: Gerald Okonjo, plot-holder of 22 years
viewpoints.text: My objection is not sentiment about full plots, which is what people assume. It is that halving works once. You cannot halve again, so it buys perhaps a decade and then the list rebuilds, and meanwhile the council has stopped looking for new land because the pressure came off. If splitting is paired with acquiring a new site I am for it. If it is used instead of acquiring one, it is a way of appearing to solve a problem while the underlying supply stays exactly where it was.

viewpoints.name: Dr Saoirse Lindqvist, urban researcher
viewpoints.text: The productivity argument against splitting is weaker than plot-holders believe. Yield per square metre on half plots is consistently higher, because smaller plots are cultivated more intensively and abandoned less often. What the argument gets right is something else: turnover on half plots is higher, and each turnover costs the site an experienced grower and costs the new tenant a season of learning. The trade-off is real, it is just not the one usually stated, and both sides tend to argue past it.

viewpoints.name: Bettina Marchetti, site secretary
viewpoints.text: Nobody in this debate mentions the shed, the water butt, the fruit bushes and the six years of soil improvement that a departing tenant leaves behind. When we split a plot we frequently split those too, and the rules say nothing about who owns them or whether the outgoing tenant is compensated. I have mediated four disputes about a greenhouse. Decide the policy by all means — but write down what happens to what people have built before you divide it, because that is where the actual conflict occurs.
